title: 是 (shì) — To Be
explanation: 是 (shì) is the verb 'to be'. It links a subject to a noun or noun phrase. Unlike English, 是 is NOT used before adjectives — use 很 instead.
notes: Don't say 天气是好 ✗. Use 天气很好 ✓. 是 is only for nouns, not adjectives.

exercises.explain: 是 links a subject to a noun: 我是学生.
是 links 这 to the noun phrase 我的书.

exercises.english: The weather is very nice today.
exercises.explain: Adjectives don't take 是. Use 很 + adjective: 天气很好.
Subject + 是 + noun. 很 only goes before adjectives.

title: 不是 (bú shì) — Negative 'To Be'
explanation: Place 不 before 是 to negate it. 不 (bù) becomes bú before a 4th-tone syllable in speech, but the character stays 不 in writing.

examples.pinyin: Zhè bú shì wǒ de shū.

exercises.english: I'm not a teacher, I'm a student.
exercises.explain: 是 is always negated with 不, never 没.
不是 = is not.
不 goes before 是: 她不是医生.
Negate 是 with 不, placed before it. 没是 is never correct.

title: 有 / 没有 — Have / Don't Have
explanation: 有 (yǒu) means 'have' or 'there is/are'. Its only negation is 没有 (méiyǒu) — never 不有. 有 also expresses existence.

examples.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng yǒu yī běn shū.
examples.english: There is a book on the table.

notes: NEVER say 不有 ✗ — the negation of 有 is always 没有.

exercises.explain: 有 = to have.
有 is negated with 没, never 不: 没有.
有没有 is the 'have or not' question form.

exercises.english: There is nobody in the room.
exercises.explain: Place + 没有 + noun = there isn't any… . 不有 does not exist.

exercises.english: There are no books on the table.

title: 很 + Adjective — Predicate Adjectives
explanation: Adjectives in Chinese can be predicates without 是. They are usually preceded by 很 (hěn). In this position 很 is often grammatically required rather than meaning 'very'.

examples.pinyin: Zhè běn shū hěn yǒu yìsi.

notes: Omitting 很 implies a comparison: 今天天气好 can mean 'today's weather is good (compared to yesterday)'.

exercises.explain: Subject + 很 + adjective. No 是 before adjectives.
Adjectives are negated with plain 不: 不大.
很 links the subject to an adjective (好吃).
很 comes before the adjective; 是 is not used with adjectives.

title: 的 (de) — Possessive / Attributive
explanation: 的 (de) marks possession (like 's in English) and links adjectives or clauses to nouns.
notes: With close relationships 的 can be dropped: 我妈妈 is natural for 'my mum'.

exercises.explain: 的 marks possession: 我的书.
的 links a describing word to the noun: 红色的衣服.

exercises.english: Who is that person wearing white?
exercises.explain: A whole phrase can describe a noun with 的: 穿白衣服的人.
Owner + 的 + thing: 老师的书.

title: 吗 (ma) — Yes/No Questions
explanation: Add 吗 to the end of any statement to make it a yes/no question. No word-order change is needed.

exercises.explain: Add 吗 to the end of a statement to make a yes/no question.
吗 goes at the very end of the sentence.
吗 always comes last.
Use either 吗 or the A-not-A form (忙不忙), never both.

title: 不 (bù) — Negation
explanation: 不 negates verbs and adjectives in the present/future or for general statements. For past actions, use 没 instead.

examples.pinyin: Tā bú shì wǒ de péngyǒu.

notes: Use 没 for past actions: 我没去 ✓ (I didn't go). 不 is for habit, present, and future.

exercises.explain: Habits and preferences are negated with 不.

exercises.english: I'm not going to school tomorrow.
exercises.explain: Future plans use 不. 没 is for things that didn't happen.
是 is always negated with 不.
Past actions are negated with 没, and 了 is dropped. 不去了 means 'not going any more'.

title: 也 (yě) — Also / Too
explanation: 也 means 'also' or 'too' and always comes BEFORE the verb — never at the end of a sentence.
notes: 我也去 ✓ (I'm also going). NOT 我去也 ✗ — 也 goes before the verb, not after.

exercises.english: I'm a student, and he is a student too.
exercises.explain: 也 = also. It goes after the subject.

exercises.english: I'm not going, and she isn't either.
exercises.explain: 也 + 不 = not … either.
也 comes before 很 + adjective: 也很忙.
也 always sits after the subject and before the verb, never at the start.

title: 都 (dōu) — All / Both
explanation: 都 means 'all' or 'both' and must come BEFORE the verb. The subject it refers to must precede 都.

examples.english: Both she and I are going.

notes: 他们都来了 ✓, not 都他们来了 ✗ — the subject must come first.

exercises.explain: 都 = all. It goes after the subject (which is plural).
都不 = none of them.
都 goes after the subject and before the verb.

exercises.english: Not all of them are students.
exercises.explain: 不都 = not all. 都不 = none at all.

title: 在 (zài) — Location
explanation: 在 marks location ('be at / in'). It can also act as a preposition before a verb phrase: 我在北京工作 (I work in Beijing).

examples.english: The book is on the table.

exercises.explain: 在 + place = to be at a place.
在 + place comes before the verb.

exercises.english: Your phone is on the table.
exercises.explain: Thing + 在 + place = the thing is located there.
Subject + 在 + place + verb.

exercises.english: My mum works at a hospital.
The cat is under the chair.

title: 了 (le) — Completion
explanation: 了 after a verb marks a completed action. It is about completion, not strictly past tense — a future action can also be 'completed'.
notes: 了 at sentence-end can also signal a change of state: 他来了 means 'He has arrived (he wasn't here before)'.

exercises.explain: Verb + 了 marks a completed action.
已经 … 了 = already done.
了吗 asks whether something has happened.
Negate a completed action with 没 and drop 了.

exercises.english: I drank two cups of coffee.

title: Measure Words (量词 liàngcí)
explanation: A measure word must sit between a number and a noun. Different nouns require different measure words. 个 (gè) is the most common and works as a fallback.

examples.english: one cup of tea (杯 for cups)
five sheets of paper (张 for flat things)

notes: Use 两 (liǎng) not 二 (èr) before measure words: 两个 ✓, 二个 ✗.

exercises.explain: 本 is the measure word for books.

exercises.english: There's a sheet of paper on the table.
exercises.explain: 张 is for flat things: paper, tables, tickets.
只 is used for most animals.

exercises.english: I bought an item of clothing.
exercises.explain: 件 is for clothes (tops) and matters/things.
Use 两 (not 二) before a measure word, and the measure word goes between the number and the noun.

exercises.english: I'd like to buy a cup of coffee.

title: 想 (xiǎng) — Want To
explanation: 想 before a verb expresses desire: 'want to' or 'would like to'. It is a modal verb followed directly by another verb.

examples.english: I want to go to Beijing.
What do you want to eat?

exercises.english: I want to go to China.
exercises.explain: 想 + verb = would like to / want to.
想 comes directly before the verb.

exercises.english: What do you want to eat?
exercises.explain: 想 is followed by a verb: 想吃.
Negate 想 with 不, placed before it.

exercises.english: I'd like a glass of water.
Where do you want to go?

title: 能 vs 会 — Two Ways to Say 'Can'
explanation: Both mean 'can' but differ: 会 (huì) = learned skill (know how to); 能 (néng) = circumstantial or physical ability (be able to in this situation).

examples.english: Can you help me? (is it possible?)

notes: If you learned it → 会. If it depends on the situation or physical possibility → 能.

exercises.english: I can speak Chinese (I've learned it).
exercises.explain: 会 = can, as a learned skill.

exercises.english: I'm busy tomorrow, so I can't come.
exercises.explain: 能 = able to, given the circumstances. 不会来 would mean 'won't come'.
能 also asks about permission.
Swimming is a learned skill, so use 会 before the verb.

exercises.english: My mum can cook Chinese food.

title: Time Word Position
pattern: Time + Subject + Verb  OR  Subject + Time + Verb
explanation: Time words in Chinese are flexible — they go at the sentence start or after the subject. They can NEVER go after the verb.

examples.english: Tomorrow he'll come to my home.

notes: 我去学校今天 ✗ — time words cannot go at the end of a sentence.

exercises.explain: Time words go before the verb, never at the end like in English.
每天 goes before the verb.

exercises.english: He gets up at eight every day.
exercises.explain: Time word + time + verb: 每天八点起床.

exercises.english: I'm going to school tomorrow morning.
She has class at three in the afternoon.
We eat dinner at seven in the evening.

title: 比 (bǐ) — Comparison
explanation: 比 compares two things. The adjective describes A relative to B. Do NOT use 很 before the adjective in a 比 sentence.
notes: 他比我很高 ✗ — no 很 in comparisons. For 'much taller' say 他比我高多了.

exercises.explain: A + 比 + B + adjective.

exercises.english: I'm two years older than him.
exercises.explain: The exact difference goes after the adjective: 大两岁.
Don't use 很 in a 比 sentence.

exercises.english: My brother is much taller than me.
exercises.explain: To say 'much more', add 多了 or 得多 after the adjective.

exercises.english: This one is cheaper than that one.
Flying is faster than taking the train.

title: 从...到... — From...To...
explanation: 从 (cóng) means 'from' and 到 (dào) means 'to'. Together they express a range of place, time, or amount.

examples.pinyin: Cóng Běijīng dào Shànghǎi hěn yuǎn.
examples.english: From Beijing to Shanghai is very far.

examples.chinese: 我从早上八点到下午五点工作。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ cóng zǎoshang bā diǎn dào xiàwǔ wǔ diǎn gōngzuò.
examples.english: I work from 8 am to 5 pm.

exercises.english: I work from nine to five.
exercises.explain: 从 … 到 … = from … to …

exercises.prompt: 从北京＿＿上海要多长时间？
exercises.english: How long does it take from Beijing to Shanghai?
exercises.explain: 从 A 到 B.

exercises.english: Is it far from here to there?
exercises.explain: 从这儿到那儿 = from here to there.

exercises.english: I work from Monday to Friday.
options: 我从星期一到星期五工作。
我到星期一从星期五工作。
我工作星期一从到星期五。
exercises.answer: 我从星期一到星期五工作。
exercises.explain: 从 … 到 … goes before the verb.

exercises.english: It takes me half an hour from home to the office.
alt: 从家到公司我要半个小时

exercises.english: The shop is open from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

title: 因为...所以... — Because...Therefore...
explanation: 因为 (yīnwèi) = 'because', 所以 (suǒyǐ) = 'therefore / so'. In Chinese both halves are often stated together, unlike English where you only use one.

examples.pinyin: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ bù qù.
examples.english: Because it's raining, I won't go.

examples.chinese: 因为我很忙，所以我没来。
examples.pinyin: Yīnwèi wǒ hěn máng, suǒyǐ wǒ méi lái.
examples.english: Because I was busy, I didn't come.

notes: You can use either word alone, but using both is the most natural pattern.

exercises.english: Because it rained, I didn't go.
exercises.explain: 因为 introduces the reason.

exercises.english: He was ill, so he didn't come to class.
exercises.explain: 所以 introduces the result.

exercises.prompt: 我今天很忙，＿＿不能去看电影。
exercises.english: I'm busy today, so I can't go to the cinema.
exercises.explain: 所以 can be used on its own for the result.

exercises.english: Because I'm tired, I want to sleep.
options: 因为我很累，所以我想睡觉。
所以我很累，因为我想睡觉。
因为我很累，但是我想睡觉。
exercises.answer: 因为我很累，所以我想睡觉。
exercises.explain: Reason first with 因为, result second with 所以.

exercises.english: Because it was too expensive, I didn't buy it.
Because it's raining today, we're not going to the park.
alt: 今天因为下雨所以我们不去公园

title: 但是 (dànshì) — But / However
explanation: 但是 connects two contrasting ideas. The shorter 但 (dàn) is also common, especially in writing.

examples.pinyin: Tā hěn máng, dànshì hěn gāoxìng.
examples.english: He is very busy, but very happy.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dànshì méiyǒu shíjiān.
examples.english: I want to go, but I don't have time.

exercises.prompt: 这件衣服很漂亮，＿＿太贵了。
exercises.english: This item of clothing is pretty, but too expensive.
exercises.explain: 但是 introduces a contrast.

exercises.english: I want to go, but I don't have time.
exercises.explain: 有 is negated with 没.

exercises.english: He speaks Chinese, but not very well.
exercises.explain: 但是 starts the second clause.

exercises.english: Chinese is hard, but very interesting.
options: 中文很难，但是很有意思。
中文很难，所以很有意思。
但是中文很难，很有意思。
exercises.answer: 中文很难，但是很有意思。
exercises.explain: 但是 goes at the start of the second clause.

exercises.english: This restaurant is small, but the food is delicious.

title: 一边...一边... — Doing Two Things at Once
pattern: Subject + 一边 + Verb1，一边 + Verb2
explanation: 一边...一边... expresses two simultaneous actions: 'while doing X, also doing Y'. Both verbs should be ongoing activities.

examples.chinese: 他一边吃饭，一边看电视。
examples.pinyin: Tā yībiān chīfàn, yībiān kàn diànshì.

examples.chinese: 我喜欢一边听音乐，一边学习。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuān yībiān tīng yīnyuè, yībiān xuéxí.
examples.english: I like studying while listening to music.

exercises.explain: 一边 A 一边 B: both parts need 一边.

exercises.prompt: 我喜欢一边听音乐一边＿＿。
exercises.english: I like doing homework while listening to music.
exercises.explain: Each 一边 is followed by an action verb.
Repeat 一边 before the second action.
Subject first, then 一边 + verb, 一边 + verb.

alt: 他一边看书一边喝咖啡

exercises.english: Don't talk on the phone while driving.
alt: 不要一边打电话一边开车

title: 正在 (zhèngzài) — Progressive
explanation: 正在 marks an action in progress right now, like the English '-ing' form. 呢 can optionally follow for extra emphasis.

exercises.english: I'm eating right now, wait a moment.
exercises.explain: 正在 + verb = in the middle of doing.
呢 often ends a 正在 sentence.
在 alone can also mark an ongoing action.
Negate an ongoing action with 没 (在), not 不.

exercises.english: When I called, he was in class.

title: 先...然后... — First...Then...
explanation: 先 (xiān) = 'first', 然后 (ránhòu) = 'then / afterwards'. Together they sequence two actions.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiān chīfàn, ránhòu qù xuéxiào.
examples.english: I'll eat first, then go to school.

examples.pinyin: Xiān xiě zuòyè, ránhòu kàn diànshì.
examples.english: Do homework first, then watch TV.

exercises.english: Let's eat first, then go to the cinema.
exercises.explain: 先 … 然后 … = first … then …

exercises.english: Wash your hands first, then eat.
exercises.explain: 先 marks the first step.

exercises.prompt: 我先去银行，然后＿＿去超市。
exercises.english: I'll go to the bank first, then the supermarket.
exercises.explain: 然后再 is a common pairing for the next step.

exercises.english: Do your homework first, then play.
exercises.explain: 先 for the first action, 然后 for the next.

exercises.english: Go straight first, then turn right.

title: 还是 (háishi) — Or (in Questions)
explanation: 还是 is used in choice questions ('A or B?'). It is different from 或者 (huòzhě), which is 'or' in statements.

examples.english: Do you drink tea or coffee?
Are you going to Beijing or Shanghai?

notes: 还是 = 'or' in questions. 或者 = 'or' in statements. Don't mix them up.

exercises.english: Do you drink tea or coffee?
exercises.explain: In questions, 'or' is 还是. 或者 is for statements.

exercises.english: Shall we go today or tomorrow?
exercises.explain: A 还是 B asks the listener to choose.
还是 questions don't take 吗.

exercises.english: I'll go on Saturday or Sunday (either is fine).
options: 我星期六或者星期天去。
我星期六还是星期天去。
我星期六和还是星期天去。
exercises.answer: 我星期六或者星期天去。
exercises.explain: In a statement, 'or' is 或者.

exercises.english: Do you want rice or noodles?
Is this one better or that one?
